title: What Marcus kept returning to
hookLine: death, the whole, duty, kindness, the present: themes on nearly every page

lines: THE SONGS THAT ALWAYS COME BACK.
cards: Look at a musician's setlist over twenty years and you'll see it: new songs come and go, but three or four always come back.
Same with a friend who tells stories, and with plenty of journals: the same two worries, the same hope, in new clothes. Marcus left twelve books with no sign of an outline.
And yet, read straight through, the way we just did, the notebook keeps circling back to the same handful of things.

teach.h: DEATH CUTS THINGS DOWN TO SIZE.
teach.b: Five themes keep coming back. First, death. Not morbidly.

Marcus reminds himself, again and again, that Alexander and his mule driver ended up the same, that the emperors before him are gone, that he will be too. Death is his tool for cutting things down to size.
Second, the whole. He keeps zooming out: you're a part of a larger nature, a limb of one body, a citizen of the world-city. What happens to you is also happening to the whole.
Third, duty. Get up in the morning, he tells himself at the start of book five, to do the work of a human being. Do the next right thing, as a Roman and a human being.
Fourth, kindness. People who wrong you are kin, acting from ignorance; correct them gently, or bear with them. He writes it so often that some readers suspect he needed it.
Fifth, the present. The only life anyone loses is the one they're living now; the past and future aren't in your hands. Here's the striking part.
These aren't five separate lessons. They feed each other. Death shrinks your grievances, which makes kindness easier.

teach.h: THE WHOLE, AND YOUR DUTY IN IT.
teach.b: The whole gives duty its point.
The present is where any of it can actually happen.

teach.h: THE PRESENT, WHERE IT ALL HAPPENS.
teach.b: That's why a notebook with no plan still holds together.
The scholar Pierre Hadot argued it isn't a collection of new thoughts at all, but the same few rules practiced over and over, rewritten until they sink in.

how: Some readers of the Meditations pick one of Marcus's recurring themes, such as death, the whole, duty, kindness or the present, and return to it daily as he did.

o: a Stoic teacher who lent Marcus his first philosophy books
the scholar who read the Meditations as rules practiced over and over
the editor who first printed the Meditations in 1559

games.q: what Marcus kept returning to. tap the pairs.
p: you're a limb of one body
wrongdoers are kin, acting from ignorance

s: Marcus wrote the Meditations from a careful outline of topics
there's no sign of an outline; the themes come back because he kept practicing them.
Alexander and his mule driver ending up the same is one of Marcus's death reminders
he uses it to cut ambition down to size.
Pierre Hadot read the Meditations as the same few rules practiced again and again
rewritten until they sink in, rather than new ideas.

games.q: you're Marcus, furious at a colleague. which of your themes do you reach for to make kindness easier?
o: death: you'll both be gone soon.
games.why: Marcus's themes feed each other: remembering death shrinks a grievance, which clears room for kindness.

practice: Run through Marcus's five slowly, death, the whole, duty, kindness, the present, and notice which one tugs at you, or whether your theme is something else, the thing your own worries keep circling back to.
Pick just one, and let it sit with you for the rest of this minute.

wordCard.voice: Pierre Hadot. The scholar who argued the Meditations aren't new ideas but the same few rules, practiced again until they sink in. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: notes, reminders. The kind of personal notebook some scholars, Hadot among them, think the Meditations were.

carryVoice: Your line: my theme. Twelve books, and a handful of themes to carry. Day six hundred thirty-eight, done.
